citation: Tam, Katy Y. Y., Wijnand A. P. van Tilburg, Christian S. Chan, Eric R. Igou, and Hakwan Lau. "Attention Drifting In and Out: The Boredom Feedback Model." Personality and Social Psychology Review 25, no. 3 (2021): 251-272. https://doi.org/10.1177/10888683211010297.
discipline: personality and social psychology, integrating attentional, functional, and cognitive-appraisal accounts of boredom into a single feedback-loop model
thesis: Synthesizing established and emerging research, the authors propose the Boredom Feedback Model (BFM): boredom is a psychological feedback loop centered on attention shifts instigated by inadequate attentional engagement (IAE) -- the discrepancy between one's actual (objectively measurable) and subjectively desired levels of attentional engagement. BFM integrates attentional, functional, and cognitive-appraisal accounts to resolve five unresolved issues: boredom coping, the boredom-self-control relationship, the joint role of attention and meaning (contra Westgate & Wilson's MAC model), boredom's co-occurrence with both high- and low-arousal emotions, and the nature of chronic boredom (boredom proneness).

sections.title: Abstract, keywords, and introduction
sections.summary: Introduces boredom as a familiar yet non-trivial emotion; credits Eastwood et al. (2012) with establishing attentional-engagement failure as a salient boredom feature; previews BFM as a feedback loop centered on attention shifts caused by IAE.

sections.title: Existing Theoretical Models on Boredom
sections.summary: Surveys Attentional Accounts (Leary et al. 1986; Fisher 1993/1998; Damrad-Frye & Laird 1989; Eastwood et al. 2012's unfulfilled-desire reframing; Eastwood & Gorelik's 2019 UCP model), Functional Accounts (Carver & Scheier; meaning-threat account; Bench & Lench 2013; Elpidorou 2014/2018a; Westgate & Wilson's 2018 MAC model), and Cognitive Appraisal Accounts (Smith & Ellsworth 1985; Van Tilburg & Igou; Pekrun's 2006 control-value theory).

sections.title: Five Unresolved Issues
sections.summary: Poses the organizing questions: boredom coping/regulation; the boredom-self-control relationship; how attention and meaning relate; why boredom co-occurs with high- and low-arousal emotions; what constitutes chronic boredom/boredom proneness. Includes Figure 1, the BFM diagram.

sections.title: BFM
sections.summary: Presents the model's components: IAE as Key Condition (DAN vs. DMN activity or dual-task inference); Antecedents of Boredom (Scenario 1 'something to do' -- attentional resource x intention to attend, Figure 2; task characteristics/appraisals; internal factors; Scenario 2 'nothing in particular to do'); Experiences of Boredom; Consequences of Boredom (attention shifts out/inward/back); and the Feedback Loop proper.

sections.title: BFM's Answers to the Five Unresolved Issues
sections.summary: Applies BFM to each open question: coping via operant/classical conditioning; self-control via integration of strength/process/construal-level models; meaning-attention-boredom relations contra the MAC model; arousal/other-emotion co-occurrence; chronic boredom via trait-attentional vs. long-term non-trait factors.

sections.title: The Explanatory Advantages of BFM
sections.summary: Compares BFM against functional models, attentional accounts, the MAC model, and Pekrun's control-value theory.

sections.title: Summary and Future Directions
sections.summary: Restates the model; offers five concrete, testable hypotheses for future research (nothing-to-do boredom, arousal fluctuation, chronic-boredom profiles, IAE vs. meaning per se, conditioned avoidance).

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Restates BFM's five explanatory contributions regarding coping, self-control, attention/meaning integration, emotion co-occurrence, and chronic boredom.

sections.title: Declarations, funding, ORCID, notes, and references
sections.summary: Conflict-of-interest and funding declarations (Hong Kong RGC GRF Grant 17610619); author notes distinguishing intention-to-attend from desired engagement level; full reference list.

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: adopted as organizing distinction; the paper 'focuses on boredom as a transient affective state,' reserving trait boredom (boredom proneness) for separate treatment under chronic boredom

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: independently theorized in 'Implications for Chronic Boredom'; bifurcated into trait-like attentional weakness vs. malleable, non-trait 'long-term factors' (e.g., lacking a compelling life goal) -- a distinction the authors say prior research had not drawn

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: named as one of three attention-shift routes ('turn inward, e.g., mind-wandering, self-reflection'); independently correlated with boredom proneness (positive) and flow proneness (negative)

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: the conceptual core of BFM: IAE is defined as the discrepancy between actual and desired attentional engagement, operationalized via DAN/DMN network balance or dual-task performance cost

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: BFM explicitly positioned as consistent with and complementary to functional accounts (Bench & Lench 2013; Elpidorou 2018a; Van Tilburg & Igou 2012); boredom 'serves a vital function of prompting individuals to direct their attention to... something that is of value'

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: 'optimal engagement' is the paper's foundational premise ('humans desire to be optimally engaged'); flow proneness appears once as a negative boredom-proneness correlate (citing Harris, 2000)

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: both treated at length as cognitive-appraisal antecedents of IAE, each independently lowering one's 'intention to attend' (repetition/O'Hanlon 1981, Daschmann et al. 2011; meaninglessness/Fahlman et al. 2009, Van Tilburg & Igou)

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: listed among boredom's characteristic experiential features ('time passing slowly,' citing London & Monello 1974, Martin et al. 2006) but not developed into an independent mechanism

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.treatment: Multidimensional State Boredom Scale (Fahlman et al., 2013); Boredom Proneness Scale (Farmer & Sundberg, 1986); pre/post-block self-report ratings (Hunter & Eastwood, 2016); qualitative interview self-report (Harris, 2000)

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.treatment: dual-task inference (reaction-time slowing, error-rate increase) proposed as a behavioral index of attentional engagement; Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) attentional errors correlated with self-reported boredom before/after task blocks (Hunter & Eastwood, 2016)

measures.label: heart rate / HRV (+ skin conductance, unlisted sub-type)
measures.treatment: rising heart rate and falling skin conductance reported as psychophysiological correlates of boredom, the inverse of the engaged-attention profile (Merrifield & Danckert, 2014)

measures.label: general neuroimaging (fMRI DAN/DMN/anterior-insula) -- not an EEG-specific measure named in this source
measures.treatment: Danckert & Merrifield's (2018) four-condition fMRI study: anticorrelated DMN/anterior-insula activation common to both boredom-induction and sustained-attention conditions, distinct from the interest-mood condition; DMN activation used to index internally-directed (vs. externally-directed) attention

readings.claim: IAE -- the discrepancy between actual and subjectively desired levels of attentional engagement -- is a key condition for boredom that instigates the attention shifts forming the feedback process underlying the emotion.

Attentional errors on the Sustained Attention to Response Task correlate with self-reported boredom both before and after task blocks (Hunter & Eastwood, 2016), and boredom shares the anticorrelated DMN/anterior-insula fMRI signature of sustained attention rather than the interest-mood condition (Danckert & Merrifield, 2018).

Even 'objectively' high-engagement, high-demand activities (video games, piloting drones) can still produce boredom if the desired level of engagement exceeds the actual level; IAE, not low engagement per se, is the operative condition.

Boredom antecedents bifurcate into IAE 'with something to do' (governed by attentional resource x intention to attend x task characteristics x appraisals x internal factors -- only the high-resource/high-intention quadrant avoids boredom) and IAE 'with nothing in particular to do' (absence of both constraint and a desired target of engagement).

When bored, attention shifts along three non-mutually-exclusive routes -- outward, inward, or back to the source -- and if the resulting attentional target remains inadequate, the loop recurs; the loop amplifies over time through operant/classical conditioning until a mere drop in engagement becomes a sufficient conditioned stimulus for avoidance.

Contra Westgate and Wilson's (2018) MAC model, which treats attention and meaning as orthogonal predictors permitting 'meaningless boredom' under full engagement, BFM holds it is impossible to feel bored while adequately engaged; meaning operates as a precursor to IAE, not an independent axis.

The boredom-self-control relationship is explained by integrating three ego-depletion mechanisms (strength model resource-depletion; process model have-to/want-to priority shift; construal-level account of low- vs. high-level construals); some ego-depletion findings may actually reflect failure to attain IAE rather than prior self-control effort.

Whether boredom manifests as high-arousal (frustration, anger, anxiety) or low-arousal (apathy, sadness, loneliness) depends on where repeated failed attentional engagement directs attention -- e.g., rumination yields low-arousal states, reaching out to others yields loneliness upon realizing relational discrepancies.

Chronic boredom (boredom proneness) reflects sustained dysfunction of the feedback loop, attributable to two distinguishable factors -- trait-like attentional weakness and non-trait 'long-term factors' (not knowing what one wants to engage with in life, or being unable to pursue it) -- with divergent intervention implications (attention training vs. life-goal/meaning-focused intervention).

BFM does not seek to substitute past work but to supplement it as part of an integrative account; it is consistent with functional models (Bench & Lench 2013; Elpidorou 2018a; Van Tilburg & Igou 2012) while offering a dynamic, multi-component process account those models do not.

interlocutors.name: Eastwood, John D., Frischen, Alexandra, Fenske, Mark J., & Smilek, Daniel (2012)
interlocutors.role: 'The unengaged mind'; establishes attentional-engagement failure and unfulfilled desire as boredom's core, foundational premise BFM builds on directly

interlocutors.name: Eastwood, John D., & Gorelik, Danielle (2019)
interlocutors.role: Unused Cognitive Potential (UCP) model -- 'desire bind' + 'unoccupied mind'; helpful bridge between attentional and functional theories, also source of 'humans desire to be optimally engaged' premise

interlocutors.name: Westgate, Erin C., & Wilson, Timothy D. (2018)
interlocutors.role: Meaning and Attentional Components (MAC) model; BFM's primary theoretical foil on the attention-meaning relationship

interlocutors.name: Elpidorou, Andreas (2014, 2018a)
interlocutors.role: regulatory meta-model of boredom (functional account); BFM positions itself as consistent with and complementary to this account

interlocutors.name: Elpidorou, Andreas (2018b)
interlocutors.role: 'The good of boredom'; source of the proposition that boredom proneness may be a dysfunction of state boredom, which BFM's chronic-boredom account is consistent with

interlocutors.name: Bench, Shane W., & Lench, Heather C. (2013)
interlocutors.role: boredom as signal and driving force for pursuit of alternative goals; functional account BFM aligns with

interlocutors.name: Pekrun, Reinhard (2006)
interlocutors.role: control-value theory of achievement emotions; BFM 'in line with' its value/control appraisal account of academic boredom

interlocutors.name: Smith, Craig A., & Ellsworth, Phoebe C. (1985)
interlocutors.role: earliest cognitive-appraisal profile of boredom (low control, low uncertainty, low effort, low attention)

interlocutors.name: Fisher, Cynthia D. (1993, 1998, 1987)
interlocutors.role: three-cause taxonomy (external, internal, interaction) of workplace boredom; attentional account emphasizing effortful maintenance of attention

interlocutors.name: Leary, Mark R., et al. (1986)
interlocutors.role: early attentional account: boredom as 'affective consequence of effortful maintenance of attention'

interlocutors.name: Danckert, James, & Merrifield, Colleen (2018)
interlocutors.role: fMRI study establishing DMN/anterior-insula anticorrelation as shared signature of boredom and sustained attention

interlocutors.name: Hunter, Amara, & Eastwood, John D. (2016)
interlocutors.role: SART study linking attentional errors to self-reported boredom pre/post task block

interlocutors.name: Merrifield, Colleen, & Danckert, James (2014)
interlocutors.role: psychophysiological (heart rate, skin conductance) correlates of boredom

interlocutors.name: Farmer, Richard, & Sundberg, Norman D. (1986)
interlocutors.role: originators of the Boredom Proneness Scale/construct

interlocutors.name: Fahlman, Shelley A., et al. (2009, 2013)
interlocutors.role: Multidimensional State Boredom Scale; life-meaning and boredom-proneness longitudinal findings

interlocutors.name: Baumeister, Roy F., & Vohs, Kathleen D. (2016)
interlocutors.role: strength model of self-regulation, one of three self-control mechanisms BFM integrates

interlocutors.name: Inzlicht, Michael, & Schmeichel, Brandon J. (2012)
interlocutors.role: process model of self-control (have-to/want-to priority shift), one of three mechanisms BFM integrates

interlocutors.name: Fujita, Kentaro (2008)
interlocutors.role: construal-level account of self-control, one of three mechanisms BFM integrates

interlocutors.name: Wolff, Wanja, & Martarelli, Corinna S. (2020)
interlocutors.role: proposal that boredom confounds ego-depletion research; BFM engages this emerging discourse

interlocutors.name: Milyavskaya, Marina, et al. (2019)
interlocutors.role: boredom-ego-depletion confound speculation; heightened reward sensitivity under boredom

interlocutors.name: Struk, Andriy A., et al. (2017, 2020)
interlocutors.role: boredom-proneness/mind-wandering association; empty-room vs. affordance-rich-room boredom-induction study supporting the desired-engagement-level mechanism

interlocutors.name: Van Tilburg, Wijnand A. P., & Igou, Eric R. (2011, 2012, 2016, 2017a, 2017b, 2019)
interlocutors.role: meaning-threat/functional account of boredom (co-authors of the present paper); repeatedly cited for the meaninglessness-boredom link and boredom's symbolic/social consequences

interlocutors.name: Chan, Christian S., et al. (2018)
interlocutors.role: situational meaninglessness and state boredom (co-author of the present paper); meaning-threat account

tensions.axis: BFM (IAE as sufficient condition; meaning as precursor to IAE) vs. MAC model (attention and meaning as orthogonal, independent predictors)
tensions.note: Westgate & Wilson's (2018) claim that 'meaningless boredom' can occur under full attentional engagement is directly contested; BFM argues this is empirically inconclusive given how 'attention' was operationalized in the MAC studies (mind-wandering tendency rather than task-related sustained-attention measures).

tensions.axis: boredom as high-arousal vs. low-arousal vs. mixed/fluctuating emotion
tensions.note: the literature offers conflicting characterizations (Smith & Ellsworth 1985 vs. Merrifield & Danckert 2014 vs. Danckert, Hammerschmidt et al. 2018); BFM resolves this by making arousal direction contingent on where post-IAE attention is directed, not a fixed property of boredom itself.

tensions.axis: boredom as genuine causal antecedent of self-control failure vs. boredom as a confound in ego-depletion research
tensions.note: Wolff & Martarelli (2020) and Milyavskaya et al. (2019) raise the possibility that boredom itself, rather than depleted self-control resources, drives 'ego-depletion' effects; BFM proposes ego-depletion may in some cases reduce to failure to attain IAE.

tensions.axis: boredom proneness as a unitary stable trait vs. BFM's bifurcation into trait-attentional and malleable long-term factors
tensions.note: BFM argues some phenomena previously classified as 'trait boredom' are in fact non-personality, malleable long-term factors (e.g., lacking a compelling life goal), with different intervention implications than genuinely trait-level attentional weakness.

tensions.axis: attentional accounts (effortful-maintenance-of-attention framing) vs. Eastwood et al.'s (2012) unfulfilled-desire reframing
tensions.note: early attentional accounts (Leary et al. 1986; Fisher 1993) center on failed effortful concentration; Eastwood et al. (2012) reframe boredom around an unfulfilled desire to engage, applicable even absent any concentration effort -- BFM builds on the latter.

dataset_channels.note: BFM's behavioral operationalizations of attentional engagement -- dual-task performance cost (RT/error) and DAN/DMN network balance -- plausibly overlap with attention-focused measures a VR attention study would collect, but this source itself uses no pupillometry, gaze/eye-tracking, or EEG; any grounds-measure linkage to the dataset's actual instrumentation requires independent confirmation (P/anticipatory-application).
